questions.title: Read a wave graph
questions.prompt:
The graph shows a wave.

parts.prompt: What are the amplitude and wavelength?

options.text: Amplitude 6 cm; wavelength 40 cm
options.feedback: 6 cm is the peak-to-peak height. Amplitude starts at the centre line.

options.text: Amplitude 3 cm; wavelength 40 cm
options.feedback: The height from the centre is 3 cm; adjacent crests are 40 cm apart.

options.text: Amplitude 3 cm; wavelength 20 cm
options.feedback: 20 cm is half a cycle. Measure from one crest to the next.

questions.title: Interpret two waves in phase
questions.prompt:
The graphs show two waves, X and Y, at the same position.
Each wave has an amplitude of 2 mm.
Use the graphs to answer the questions about the waves.

parts.prompt: What is the phase difference between X and Y?

options.text: A quarter cycle apart: 90°.
options.feedback: The corresponding crests are aligned, rather than a quarter cycle apart.

options.text: They have different frequencies.
options.feedback: The same time spacing between crests shows equal frequencies.

options.text: In phase: 0°.
options.feedback: Corresponding crests and troughs occur at the same times, so the waves are in phase.

options.text: Antiphase: 180°.
options.feedback: Antiphase would put a crest of one wave opposite a trough of the other.

parts.correctFeedback: Corresponding crests and troughs occur at the same times, so the waves are in phase.

parts.prompt: Which type of interference occurs when the waves overlap?

options.text: Destructive with complete cancellation.
options.feedback: Complete cancellation needs equal amplitudes and opposite displacements.

options.text: Destructive with partial cancellation.
options.feedback: The waves are in phase, so their displacements reinforce rather than oppose.

options.text: No superposition occurs.
options.feedback: Waves superpose wherever they overlap.

options.text: Constructive.
options.feedback: The in-phase displacements reinforce each other.

parts.correctFeedback: The in-phase displacements reinforce each other.

parts.prompt: What is the amplitude of the resultant wave?

options.text: 4 mm
options.feedback: Add the equal in-phase amplitudes: 2 + 2 = 4 mm.

options.text: 2 mm
options.feedback: The original amplitude is 2 mm; superposition of these waves doubles it.

options.text: 0 mm
options.feedback: The waves reinforce each other, so the resultant is not zero.

options.text: 8 mm
options.feedback: Adding two 2 mm amplitudes gives 4 mm; 8 mm would be the peak-to-peak height.

parts.correctFeedback: Add the equal in-phase amplitudes: 2 + 2 = 4 mm.

questions.modelAnswer: The waves are in phase: their phase difference is 0°. Their displacements add, producing constructive interference. The resultant amplitude is 2 + 2 = 4 mm.
generalFeedback: The crests occur at the same times, so the waves are in phase.
In-phase displacements add: 2 + 2 = 4 mm.
questions.hint: Compare the times of corresponding crests before adding amplitudes.
sources: June 2023 Q1(b): wave-pair interpretation; guide p.100.

questions.prompt:
A string is fixed at both ends. Its length is 0.50 m and its mass per unit length, μ, is 0.0020 kg/m.

parts.prompt: Select the rearrangement for tension.

options.text: T = μ/v²
options.feedback: This rearrangement reverses the required relationship.

options.text: T = v²μ
options.feedback: Square the speed, then multiply by mass per unit length.

options.text: T = vμ
options.feedback: The speed must be squared.

options.text: T = v²/μ
options.feedback: Multiply by μ after squaring.

parts.correctFeedback: Square the speed, then multiply by mass per unit length.

parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.

questions.title: Apply the inverse-square law
questions.prompt:
A transmitter emits radio waves.
At a distance of 3.0 m, the intensity of the waves is 0.072 W/m².
Calculate the intensity at a distance of 9.0 m.
Assume that the inverse-square law applies. Use I = k/r².

parts.prompt: Calculate k using the intensity at 3.0 m.
parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.
parts.incorrectFeedback: Multiply 0.072 by 3.0².

parts.prompt: Which expression gives the intensity at 9.0 m?

options.feedback: 9.0² = 81, so divide k by 81.

options.text: I = 81k
options.feedback: This reverses the inverse-square relationship.

options.text: I = k/9
options.feedback: Square the distance before dividing.

options.text: I = 9k
options.feedback: Increasing distance should reduce intensity.

parts.correctFeedback: 9.0² = 81, so divide k by 81.

parts.prompt: Calculate the intensity at 9.0 m.
parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.
parts.incorrectFeedback: Divide k by 81.

questions.modelAnswer: k = 0.072 × 3.0² = 0.648 W. I = 0.648/9.0² = 0.648/81 = 0.0080 W/m². Tripling the distance reduces intensity by a factor of 9.
generalFeedback: Dividing by 9 instead of 81 misses the square on distance.
Intensity falls with distance under the stated model.
The ratio is (old distance/new distance)², so intensity becomes one ninth of its original value.
questions.hint: Find k from the first position. Square the second distance before dividing.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the frequency ranges of regions in the electromagnetic spectrum is correct?

parts.prompt: Which statement about the frequency ranges of regions in the electromagnetic spectrum is correct?

options.text: The frequency ranges of all regions have exact boundaries with no overlap.
options.feedback: The specification recognises overlapping frequency and wavelength ranges.

options.text: Overlapping labels mean the radiation is no longer electromagnetic.
options.feedback: A classification overlap does not change the wave nature.

options.text: Two regions can overlap only if their vacuum speeds differ.
options.feedback: All regions have the same vacuum speed.

options.text: Some neighbouring region frequency ranges overlap.
options.feedback: Region boundaries are approximate and some ranges overlap.

parts.correctFeedback: Region boundaries are approximate and some ranges overlap.

questions.title: Recall photon energy across the spectrum
questions.prompt: What happens to the energy of a photon as its frequency increases?

parts.prompt: What happens to the energy of a photon as its frequency increases?

options.text: Photon energy must stay the same.
options.feedback: Different frequencies correspond to different photon energies.

options.text: Only the wave speed increases.
options.feedback: Vacuum speed stays constant; photon energy changes.

options.text: Photon energy increases.
options.feedback: Higher-frequency photons carry more energy each.

options.text: Photon energy decreases.
options.feedback: The energy-frequency relationship increases rather than decreases.

parts.correctFeedback: Higher-frequency photons carry more energy each.

questions.modelAnswer: The energy of the photon increases as its frequency increases.

questions.hint: A higher frequency means more energy for each photon.
